Sharp noncommutative Hilbert and Riesz inequalities:
classification and spectral correctionsThanks: ∗Department of Mathematical Sciences, Tsinghua University, Beijing 100084, China.
E-mail: longzy25@mails.tsinghua.edu.cn

Zhouyu Long∗
Abstract.

For every 1<p<∞1<p<\infty, with p∗=max⁡{p,p/(p−1)}p^{*}=\max\{p,p/(p-1)\}, we determine the sharp Hilbert norm Cp=cot⁡(π/(2​p∗))C_{p}=\cot(\pi/(2p^{*})) on Lp​(ℝ,𝒮p)L^{p}(\mathbb{R};\mathcal{S}_{p}) and the sharp uniform bound Dp=csc⁡(π/p)D_{p}=\csc(\pi/p) for retained and strict Riesz projections of maximal subdiagonal algebras in finite tracial von Neumann algebras. The Hilbert value is also the common Fourier–Schur completely bounded norm. For finite matrices, a nonnegative logarithmic determinant defect connects Heinävaara’s tracial joint spectral measure to eigenvalues. The resulting transfer identity classifies finite signed real ridge inequalities on nilpotents and identifies their least additive eigenvalue corrections. A dual theorem characterizes weak-* limits of weighted angular measures of finite nilpotents. In general finite tracial algebras, separate positive-kernel and sharp determinant-covariance comparisons yield the Riesz bounds. Consequences include the sharp Volterra constant, Riesz–Titchmarsh and shifted-transform formulas, joint real-pencil norms, and exact triangular and operator-valued Fourier Riesz norms.

Key words and phrases: 
Hilbert transform, Riesz projection, Schatten class, subdiagonal algebra, spectral correction
2020 Mathematics Subject Classification
Primary 47B10; Secondary 42A50, 47A30, 46L52

1. Introduction

Throughout, 1<p<∞1<p<\infty, p′=p/(p−1)p^{\prime}=p/(p-1), and p∗=max⁡{p,p′}p^{*}=\max\{p,p^{\prime}\}. We determine the noncommutative sharp constants

Cp=cot⁡π2​p∗,Dp=csc⁡πp.C_{p}=\cot\frac{\pi}{2p^{*}},\qquad D_{p}=\csc\frac{\pi}{p}.

The Hilbert transform on Lp​(ℝ,𝒮p)L^{p}(\mathbb{R};\mathcal{S}_{p}) and the ordered Hilbert Schur multiplier have norm CpC_{p}. Every maximal subdiagonal algebra in a finite tracial von Neumann algebra has retained and strict Riesz projections bounded by DpD_{p}, optimally over this class. The first three theorems state the analytic-distance bound, the determinant-covariance estimate, and the classification with least spectral correction.

The scalar Hilbert value is due to Pichorides [14], and the real-pencil values to Hollenbeck–Kalton–Verbitsky [9]. Neuwirth–Ricard identified the Hilbert Fourier–Schur and completely bounded norms for every exponent [18, Theorem 6.2], and computed their value for powers of two and their conjugate exponents. We determine that value throughout the exponent range. The shifted-transform formula includes the Riesz–Titchmarsh conjecture at the half shift and Laeng’s full Conjecture 5.7 [12]; it extends the even-integer and conjugate-exponent cases of Bañuelos–Kwaśnicki [1]. The Volterra consequence gives the conjectured sharp comparison of the self-adjoint parts of compact quasinilpotent operators, recorded in [24]; see also the classical work [21, 22, 23].

Hollenbeck–Verbitsky determined the scalar Riesz value DpD_{p} [34]. Randrianantoanina proved boundedness for finite maximal subdiagonal algebras [33]. Neuwirth–Ricard identified the triangular Schatten norm with the completely bounded Fourier Riesz norm and computed its value at p=4p=4 [18, Proposition 6.3]; duality gives p=4/3p=4/3, besides the elementary case p=2p=2. Here the sharp uniform upper bound is proved directly in arbitrary finite tracial algebras.

The proofs use two spectral comparisons with exact nonnegative remainders. For finite matrices, our logarithmic determinant defect compares eigenvalues with Heinävaara’s positive tracial joint spectral measure [2]. The ridge transform and its one-variable differential inverse are already present in [3, Remark 2, p. 40]; the additional ingredient here is the nonnegative eigenvalue defect and its optimal spectral correction. For finite tracial algebras, logarithmic rearrangement and determinant covariance give the analytic witnesses needed for the Riesz theorem. Remark 1.8 specifies the distinct scopes of these comparisons.

1.1. Sharp Riesz bounds in finite tracial algebras

For the subdiagonal results, (ℳ,τ)(\mathcal{M},\tau) is a finite von Neumann algebra with a faithful normal tracial state and τ⁡(I)=1\tau(I)=1. For 1≤p<∞1\leq p<\infty, Lp​(ℳ)L^{p}(\mathcal{M}) is the completion of ℳ\mathcal{M} for ‖x‖p=(τ​|x|p)1/p\|x\|_{p}=(\tau|x|^{p})^{1/p}, identified with the corresponding affiliated measurable operators. We use the trace pairing ⟨x,y⟩=τ⁡(y∗​x)\langle x,y\rangle=\tau(y^{*}x), Hölder’s inequality, cyclicity for integrable products, and LpL^{p}–Lp′L^{p^{\prime}} duality, where p′=p/(p−1)p^{\prime}=p/(p-1). Since the trace is normalized, ‖x‖q≤‖x‖p\|x\|_{q}\leq\|x\|_{p} when q≤pq\leq p.

A subdiagonal algebra is a weak-star closed unital algebra ℬ⊂ℳ\mathcal{B}\subset\mathcal{M} for which 𝒟=ℬ∩ℬ∗\mathcal{D}=\mathcal{B}\cap\mathcal{B}^{*} admits a trace-preserving normal conditional expectation Φ:ℳ→𝒟\Phi:\mathcal{M}\to\mathcal{D}, multiplicative on ℬ\mathcal{B}, and ℬ+ℬ∗\mathcal{B}+\mathcal{B}^{*} is weak-star dense in ℳ\mathcal{M}. It is maximal if it is maximal among the subdiagonal algebras for the same expectation. Write ℬ0=ℬ∩ker⁡Φ\mathcal{B}_{0}=\mathcal{B}\cap\ker\Phi and

Hp=ℬ¯Lp,H0p=ℬ0¯Lp,𝒞=ℬ+ℬ0∗.H^{p}=\overline{\mathcal{B}}^{\,L^{p}},\qquad H_{0}^{p}=\overline{\mathcal{B}_{0}}^{\,L^{p}},\qquad\mathcal{C}=\mathcal{B}+\mathcal{B}_{0}^{*}.

On this bounded core the retained-diagonal projection is P⁡(U+Y)=UP(U+Y)=U and the strict projection is P0=P−ΦP_{0}=P-\Phi. Their well-definedness and core density are proved below.

Theorem 1.1.

For every maximal subdiagonal algebra in (ℳ,τ)(\mathcal{M},\tau) and every 1<p<∞1<p<\infty,

‖U+Y‖p\displaystyle\|U+Y\|_{p} ≥sin⁡πp​‖U‖p,\displaystyle\geq\sin\frac{\pi}{p}\,\|U\|_{p}, U\displaystyle U ∈Hp,Y∈(H0p)∗,\displaystyle\in H^{p},\quad Y\in(H_{0}^{p})^{*},
(1.1) ‖U0+Y0‖p\displaystyle\|U_{0}+Y_{0}\|_{p} ≥sin⁡πp​‖U0‖p,\displaystyle\geq\sin\frac{\pi}{p}\,\|U_{0}\|_{p}, U0\displaystyle U_{0} ∈H0p,Y0∈(Hp)∗.\displaystyle\in H_{0}^{p},\quad Y_{0}\in(H^{p})^{*}.

Here (Hp)∗={x∗:x∈Hp}(H^{p})^{*}=\{x^{*}:x\in H^{p}\} and similarly for H0pH_{0}^{p}. Consequently PP and P0P_{0} extend to bounded operators on Lp​(ℳ)L^{p}(\mathcal{M}), and

(1.2) ‖P‖Lp→Lp≤csc⁡πp,‖P0‖Lp→Lp≤csc⁡πp.\quad\|P\|_{L^{p}\to L^{p}}\leq\csc\frac{\pi}{p},\qquad\|P_{0}\|_{L^{p}\to L^{p}}\leq\csc\frac{\pi}{p}.\quad

The distance coefficient and both projection bounds are optimal uniformly over this class. Equality is not asserted for every individual algebra.

The new upper bound.

The scalar sharp value supplies a lower bound; the known Fourier–Schur transference relations do not supply the missing all-exponent upper bound. We prove that upper bound in the finite algebra itself. Determinant covariance handles 2<p<42<p<4; positive-kernel comparison and independently established analytic regularization handle p>4p>4. Continuity, duality, and a subdiagonal matrix construction complete the retained and strict bounds. Section 8.6 then gives the exact uniform triangular norm and the exact Fourier Riesz norm with any nonzero finite coefficient algebra (Corollaries 8.11 and 8.13).

The trace inequality below supplies the middle-exponent estimate. Here Detτ\operatorname{Det}_{\tau} is the Fuglede–Kadison determinant, with its definition and structural properties recalled in Appendix C.

Theorem 1.2.

Let (ℳ,τ)(\mathcal{M},\tau) be any finite von Neumann algebra with a faithful normal trace satisfying τ⁡(I)=1\tau(I)=1, and let N∈ℳN\in\mathcal{M} satisfy Detτ⁡(I+ζ​N)≥1\operatorname{Det}_{\tau}(I+\zeta N)\geq 1 for every ζ∈ℂ\zeta\in\mathbb{C}. Then τ​N=0\tau N=0, and for every bounded invertible D>0D>0 and 0<β<10<\beta<1,

(1.3) |τ​Dβ​N|2≤sin2⁡π​β2​(1+β)​τ​D1+β​τ​(N∗​Dβ−1​N).|\tau D^{\beta}N|^{2}\leq\sin^{2}\frac{\pi\beta}{2(1+\beta)}\,\tau D^{1+\beta}\,\tau(N^{*}D^{\beta-1}N).

When v=τ⁡(N∗​Dβ−1​N)>0v=\tau(N^{*}D^{\beta-1}N)>0, the deficit has the nonnegative entropy and determinant residual (5.26). For each fixed β\beta, the squared coefficient is optimal uniformly over normalized finite tracial algebras; this is proved after the circle construction in Section 6.3.

For N∈ℬ0N\in\mathcal{B}_{0} or N∈ℬ0∗N\in\mathcal{B}_{0}^{*}, the determinant hypothesis follows from the general Jensen inequality (Corollary 5.10). With β=(p−2)/2\beta=(p-2)/2, the squared coefficient in (1.3) is cos2⁡(π/p)\cos^{2}(\pi/p). Analytic factorization turns this covariance estimate into the L2L^{2} angle bound used for 2<p<42<p<4. The proof and residual are given in Section 5; sharpness follows from the scalar circle construction in Section 6.3.

1.2. Matrix classification and optimal spectral correction

The underlying questions are: which finite signed real ridge inequalities hold for all nilpotent matrices, and what is their least additive eigenvalue correction for arbitrary matrices? Theorem 1.3 answers both through the least homogeneous superharmonic majorant, extending the scalar analytic-test/majorant principle of [9, Theorem 2.1].

All Hilbert spaces are complex; traces are unnormalized unless specified otherwise. Let m2m_{2} denote planar Lebesgue measure and set Δ=∂x2+∂y2\Delta=\partial_{x}^{2}+\partial_{y}^{2}. We write ∥⋅∥p\|\cdot\|_{p} for the Schatten pp-norm; unadorned matrix norms are operator norms. A compact quasinilpotent operator is called a Volterra operator. The spectral mechanism.

Heinävaara’s positive tracial joint spectral measure μA,B\mu_{A,B} [2] represents real directional trace functionals. Corollary 2.6 connects it to the eigenvalues of T=A+i​BT=A+iB through a nonnegative potential ΨT\Psi_{T}: for every U∈𝒰pU\in\mathcal{U}_{p} with U≥FU\geq F,

∑kU⁡(λk​(T))−ℱp​(A,B)\displaystyle\sum_{k}U(\lambda_{k}(T))-\mathcal{F}_{p}(A,B) =p⁡(p+1)​∫ℂ(U−F)​d​μA,B\displaystyle=p(p+1)\int_{\mathbb{C}}(U-F)\,\mathrm{d}\mu_{A,B}
+12​π∫ℂΨT(−ΔU)dm2.\displaystyle+\frac{1}{2\pi}\int_{\mathbb{C}}\Psi_{T}(-\Delta U)\,\mathrm{d}m_{2}.

Both remainders are finite and nonnegative. This gives the matrix inequality, while translated Toeplitz tests establish the pointwise optimal correction (1.8). The mass of ΨT\Psi_{T} is π2​(‖T‖22−∑k|λk​(T)|2)\frac{\pi}{2}(\|T\|_{2}^{2}-\sum_{k}|\lambda_{k}(T)|^{2}), linking Henrici’s departure from normality [8] to the sharp quantitative Weyl comparison in Corollary B.3.

Angular measures and inverse realization.

Theorem 7.2 gives a converse realization theorem: a finite positive measure ν\nu on 𝕋\mathbb{T} is a weak-* limit of the weighted angular measures of single finite nilpotent matrices if and only if

ν=(∂θ2+p2)ω,ω∈C(𝕋),ω≥0.\nu=(\partial_{\theta}^{2}+p^{2})\omega,\qquad\omega\in C(\mathbb{T}),\quad\omega\geq 0.

The matrix dimensions may grow. Separately, Corollary 3.7 derives the finite directional moment cones and their optimal quotients directly from the classification by finite-dimensional separation.

At p=4p=4, Theorem 8.5 identifies the closed disk of normalized directional moments. Corollary 8.7 gives the optimal quotient in closed form for every signed numerator and every signed denominator strictly positive on this disk. The signed classification and joint norm formulas follow by substitution.

Let T=A+i​BT=A+iB be compact and quasinilpotent. If A∈𝒮pA\in\mathcal{S}_{p}, then B∈𝒮pB\in\mathcal{S}_{p} and, for every real a,ba,b,

The constants are optimal already over finite nilpotent matrices. In particular (1.24) resolves, for every 1<p<∞1<p<\infty, the conjectured sharp constant recorded by Matsaev–Sodin [24]; see also [22].

The spectral correction determines the optimal comparison constant for every nonempty prescribed spectral set.

For Ω=Σp\Omega=\Sigma_{p}, sharpness holds already over finite nilpotents.

The compact assertion assumes T∈𝒮pT\in\mathcal{S}_{p} and allows nonnormal operators. The one-component membership assumption of Corollary 1.6 is used only in the quasinilpotent setting.

Remark 1.8.

The real ridge classification concerns finite matrices and its Schatten-class consequences. Its extension to arbitrary finite von Neumann algebras would require a compatible positive ridge representation and the corresponding integrability and comparison identities. The Riesz argument establishes its stated bounds in arbitrary finite tracial algebras by a different spectral comparison; it does not supply such a representation. In particular, traces of real directional powers cannot in general be combined as scalar radial functions to recover τ​|A+i​B|p\tau|A+iB|^{p}. The real-pencil norm identities and the Riesz projection identities therefore remain complementary results. They do not assert a sharp lifting theorem for arbitrary complex pencils a​I+b​HaI+bH. For the subdiagonal projections, sharpness means optimality uniformly over algebras; for triangular truncation it means a supremum over matrix sizes. The Fourier Riesz norm equals DpD_{p} for every nonzero finite coefficient algebra.

The proofs follow two complementary routes. For finite matrices, Heinävaara’s tracial joint spectral measure and a nonnegative logarithmic determinant defect give the exact spectral transfer identity in Section 2. Analytic-disc envelopes and Toeplitz tests then yield the classification and least spectral correction in Section 3. The transfer identity and classification, together with the finite-dimensional realizations of Section 4, give the Hilbert, Volterra, and shifted-transform bounds. Section 7 establishes the angular inverse realization.

For general finite tracial algebras, the Riesz argument uses the separate comparisons in Section 5. Determinant covariance gives the analytic-distance estimate for 2<p<42<p<4, while positive-kernel comparison and independently proved analytic regularization supply the witnesses for p>4p>4. Section 6 completes the projection theorem by continuity, duality, and a subdiagonal corner construction. Section 8 collects the compact spectral, moment, and projection consequences; Section 9 explains the limits of the two-point criterion. The appendices contain the coordinate majorant, quantitative comparisons, Hardy-space structural inputs, analytic regularization, and rotation and independent-coordinate consequences.

2. A spectral transfer theorem and its homogeneous consequences

We use the following form of Heinävaara’s representation [2]. For Hermitian A,B∈Md​(ℂ)A,B\in M_{d}(\mathbb{C}) there is a positive Borel measure μA,B\mu_{A,B}, normalized by μA,B​({0})=0\mu_{A,B}(\{0\})=0, such that the following identity holds simultaneously for every s,t∈ℝs,t\in\mathbb{R} and every measurable real ff with f⁡(0)=0f(0)=0 and ∫−MM|f⁡(u)/u|​𝑑u<∞\int_{-M}^{M}|f(u)/u|\,\mathrm{d}u<\infty for each M>0M>0:

(2.1) ∫ℝ2f⁡(s​x+t​y)​d​μA,B​(x,y)=tr⁡ℋ⁡(f)​(s​A+t​B),ℋ⁡(f)​(u)=∫011−rr​f​(r​u)​𝑑r.\int_{\mathbb{R}^{2}}f(sx+ty)\,\mathrm{d}\mu_{A,B}(x,y)=\operatorname{tr}\mathcal{H}(f)(sA+tB),\qquad\mathcal{H}(f)(u)=\int_{0}^{1}\frac{1-r}{r}f(ru)\,\mathrm{d}r.

The measure is unique away from the origin [2]. Complex tests are handled by real and imaginary parts. The normalization at zero fixes the otherwise irrelevant mass there. In particular, for every q>0q>0,

(2.2) q⁡(q+1)​∫|s​x+t​y|q​d​μA,B=tr⁡|s​A+t​B|q.q(q+1)\int|sx+ty|^{q}\,\mathrm{d}\mu_{A,B}=\operatorname{tr}|sA+tB|^{q}.

For integer k≥1k\geq 1 the same tracial formula gives

(2.3) ∫(s​x+t​y)k​d​μA,B=tr⁡(s​A+t​B)kk⁡(k+1).\int(sx+ty)^{k}\,\mathrm{d}\mu_{A,B}=\frac{\operatorname{tr}(sA+tB)^{k}}{k(k+1)}.

Nonnegative one-variable tests show

(2.4) supp⁡μA,B⊂[−‖A‖,‖A‖]×[−‖B‖,‖B‖].\operatorname{supp}\mu_{A,B}\subset[-\left\lVert A\right\rVert,\left\lVert A\right\rVert]\times[-\left\lVert B\right\rVert,\left\lVert B\right\rVert].

For example, choose a nonnegative ff vanishing on [−‖A‖,‖A‖][-\left\lVert A\right\rVert,\left\lVert A\right\rVert] and strictly positive off this interval, then use (s,t)=(1,0)(s,t)=(1,0) in (2.1). The other coordinate is identical. For every q>0q>0, the elementary bound |(x,y)|q≤Cqcoord​(|x|q+|y|q)|(x,y)|^{q}\leq C_{q}^{\mathrm{coord}}(|x|^{q}+|y|^{q}), where Cqcoord=max⁡{1,2q/2−1}C_{q}^{\mathrm{coord}}=\max\{1,2^{q/2-1}\}, and (2.2) give

(2.5) ∫|(x,y)|q​d​μA,B<∞.\int|(x,y)|^{q}\,\mathrm{d}\mu_{A,B}<\infty.

Thus the tracial measure has compact support and every positive radial moment is finite, although its total mass can be infinite.

There is also an exact support-radius identity. Put T=A+i​BT=A+iB, ℓθ​(z)=Re⁡(e−i​θ​z)\ell_{\theta}(z)=\operatorname{Re}(e^{-i\theta}z) and Rθ=supz∈supp⁡μA,B∪{0}|ℓθ​(z)|R_{\theta}=\sup_{z\in\operatorname{supp}\mu_{A,B}\cup\{0\}}|\ell_{\theta}(z)|. For 0<a<Rθ0<a<R_{\theta}, continuity and the definition of support give μA,B​(Ea)>0\mu_{A,B}(E_{a})>0 for Ea={|ℓθ|>a}E_{a}=\{|\ell_{\theta}|>a\}, while a​μA,B​(Ea)≤∫|ℓθ|​d​μA,B<∞a\mu_{A,B}(E_{a})\leq\int|\ell_{\theta}|\,\mathrm{d}\mu_{A,B}<\infty. For q≥1q\geq 1,

aq​μA,B​(Ea)≤∫|ℓθ|q​d​μA,B≤Rθq−1​∫|ℓθ|​d​μA,B.a^{q}\mu_{A,B}(E_{a})\leq\int|\ell_{\theta}|^{q}\,\mathrm{d}\mu_{A,B}\leq R_{\theta}^{q-1}\int|\ell_{\theta}|\,\mathrm{d}\mu_{A,B}.

The full ridge identity (2.1), rather than only its absolute power moments, is used in the Green decomposition below; see also Example B.1.

2.1. A nonnegative logarithmic determinant defect

Logarithmic determinants and subharmonicity have long been used to compare real and imaginary parts; see [24] and the Hilbert-transform formulation in [25, Section 2]. Here the determinant Jensen formula gives the explicit nonnegative potential used in the exact spectral-defect identity. Fix a finite matrix T=A+i​BT=A+iB. For w∉spec⁡Tw\notin\operatorname{spec}T set E=T−w​IE=T-wI and define

(2.7) LT​(w)\displaystyle L_{T}(w) =d​log⁡2+12​π​∫02​πlog⁡|detRe⁡(e−i​θ​E)|​𝑑θ,\displaystyle=d\log 2+\frac{1}{2\pi}\int_{0}^{2\pi}\log\left|\det\operatorname{Re}(e^{-i\theta}E)\right|\,\mathrm{d}\theta,
(2.8) ΨT​(w)\displaystyle\Psi_{T}(w) =LT​(w)−log⁡|det(T−w​I)|.\displaystyle=L_{T}(w)-\log|\det(T-wI)|.

Values at the finitely many eigenvalues will be irrelevant to area integration.

For w∉spec⁡Tw\notin\operatorname{spec}T,

(2.9) ΨT​(w)=∑j=1dlog+⁡|λj​(E−1​E∗)|≥0.\Psi_{T}(w)=\sum_{j=1}^{d}\log^{+}\left|\lambda_{j}(E^{-1}E^{*})\right|\geq 0.

(2.10) suppΨT⊂W⁡(T)¯,W(T)={v∗Tv:v∈ℂd,∥v∥=1}.\operatorname{supp}\Psi_{T}\subset\overline{W(T)},\qquad W(T)=\{v^{*}Tv:\ v\in\mathbb{C}^{d},\ \|v\|=1\}.

In particular it vanishes for |w|>‖T‖|w|>\|T\|. On each bounded set it is bounded above by a constant plus ∑jlog−⁡|w−λj​(T)|\sum_{j}\log^{-}|w-\lambda_{j}(T)|. Moreover,

(2.11) Ψr​T​(w)=ΨT​(w/r),r>0.\Psi_{rT}(w)=\Psi_{T}(w/r),\qquad r>0.
Proof.

The determinant factorization is

detRe⁡(e−i​θ​E)=2−d​e−i​d​θ​detE​det(I+e2​i​θ​E−1​E∗).\det\operatorname{Re}(e^{-i\theta}E)=2^{-d}e^{-id\theta}\det E\,\det(I+e^{2i\theta}E^{-1}E^{*}).

For every ζ∈ℂ\zeta\in\mathbb{C},

12​π​∫02​πlog⁡|1+ζ​ei​θ|​𝑑θ=log+⁡|ζ|.\frac{1}{2\pi}\int_{0}^{2\pi}\log|1+\zeta e^{i\theta}|\,\mathrm{d}\theta=\log^{+}|\zeta|.

Factoring the characteristic polynomial, rather than diagonalizing the matrix, proves (2.9). Roots on the unit circle cause only integrable logarithmic zeros. Since EE is invertible, the determinant polynomial in e2​i​θe^{2i\theta} is not identically zero.

When w∉W⁡(T)¯w\notin\overline{W(T)}, EE is invertible because spec⁡T⊂W⁡(T)\operatorname{spec}T\subset W(T). Let E−1​E∗​v=λ​vE^{-1}E^{*}v=\lambda v, with v≠0v\neq 0. Then E∗​v=λ​E​vE^{*}v=\lambda Ev. Writing q=v∗​E​vq=v^{*}Ev, we have

|q|≥dist⁡(w,W⁡(T))​‖v‖2>0,q¯=λ​q.|q|\geq\operatorname{dist}(w,W(T))\|v\|^{2}>0,\qquad\overline{q}=\lambda q.

Thus every eigenvalue has |λ|=1|\lambda|=1, and (2.9) is zero. Applying this to each eigenvalue proves the support assertion. Eigenvalue continuity as an unordered multiset also proves continuity of ΨT\Psi_{T} off spec⁡T\operatorname{spec}T.

On a fixed bounded set, the determinant norm bound in (2.7) gives, with a sufficiently large constant MM,

0≤ΨT​(w)≤M−∑jlog⁡|w−λj​(T)|≤M′+∑jlog−⁡|w−λj​(T)|.0\leq\Psi_{T}(w)\leq M-\sum_{j}\log|w-\lambda_{j}(T)|\leq M^{\prime}+\sum_{j}\log^{-}|w-\lambda_{j}(T)|.

2.5. The sharp coordinate specialization

The sharp coordinate estimate uses the classical explicit superharmonic majorant. The obstacle classification treats general signed ridge sums and identifies their optimal spectral correction.

Corollary 2.7.

For every 1<p<∞1<p<\infty,

(2.25) supN≠0​finite​nilpotent‖Im⁡N‖p‖Re⁡N‖p=supℰ‖Hℰ‖𝒮p→𝒮p=Cp.\sup_{N\neq 0\ {\rm finite\ nilpotent}}\frac{\|\operatorname{Im}N\|_{p}}{\|\operatorname{Re}N\|_{p}}=\sup_{\mathcal{E}}\|H_{\mathcal{E}}\|_{\mathcal{S}_{p}\to\mathcal{S}_{p}}=C_{p}.

Let UpU_{p} be the sectorwise superharmonic majorant in Appendix A and put V⁡(x,y)=Up​(y,x)V(x,y)=U_{p}(y,x). Its elementary verification gives

For arbitrary XX, apply this to (0XX∗0)\left(\begin{smallmatrix}0&X\\ X^{*}&0\end{smallmatrix}\right) and the amplified flag; both ppth powers acquire the factor two. Arbitrary block sizes also give the bound at every amplification.

For sharpness, analytic polynomials qq with q⁡(0)=0q(0)=0 approach the classical Pichorides constant [14, 9]. Lemma 3.1 transfers their ratios to q⁡(Sn)q(S_{n}). These strictly upper-triangular matrices satisfy Im⁡q⁡(Sn)=Hℰ​Re⁡q⁡(Sn)\operatorname{Im}q(S_{n})=H_{\mathcal{E}}\operatorname{Re}q(S_{n}) for the standard flag, giving both lower bounds in (2.25). ∎

3. Proof of the classification and optimal correction

3.1. Finite Toeplitz sections

The lower bounds in the two parts use the same finite-section limit. Its singular-value form handles arbitrary complex symbols; its self-adjoint form supplies the continuous spectral tests needed for the nilpotent classification.

Lemma 3.1.

Let Q⁡(z)=∑k=−rrQk​zkQ(z)=\sum_{k=-r}^{r}Q_{k}z^{k} be an Md​(ℂ)M_{d}(\mathbb{C})-valued trigonometric polynomial, with dd and rr fixed, and put

An​(Q)=(Qj−i)1≤i,j≤n,n>2​r.A_{n}(Q)=(Q_{j-i})_{1\leq i,j\leq n},\qquad n>2r.

For every 1≤p<∞1\leq p<\infty,

(3.1) limn→∞1n​Trn​d​|An​(Q)|p=∫02​πTrd⁡|Q⁡(ei​t)|p​d​t2​π.\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{1}{n}\operatorname{Tr}_{nd}|A_{n}(Q)|^{p}=\int_{0}^{2\pi}\operatorname{Tr}_{d}|Q(e^{it})|^{p}\frac{dt}{2\pi}.

If Q⁡(ei​t)Q(e^{it}) is Hermitian for every tt and gg is continuous on a common interval containing the spectra of An​(Q)A_{n}(Q) and Q⁡(ei​t)Q(e^{it}), then

(3.2) limn→∞1n​Trn​d⁡g⁡(An​(Q))=∫02​πTrd⁡g⁡(Q⁡(ei​t))​d​t2​π.\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{1}{n}\operatorname{Tr}_{nd}g(A_{n}(Q))=\int_{0}^{2\pi}\operatorname{Tr}_{d}g(Q(e^{it}))\frac{dt}{2\pi}.
Proof.

Let SnS_{n} be the cyclic shift with a one at (i,j)(i,j) when j−i≡1(modn)j-i\equiv 1\pmod{n}, and set

Cn​(Q)=∑k=−rrSnk⊗Qk,R=∑k=−rr‖Qk‖.C_{n}(Q)=\sum_{k=-r}^{r}S_{n}^{k}\otimes Q_{k},\qquad R=\sum_{k=-r}^{r}\|Q_{k}\|.

The difference En=An​(Q)−Cn​(Q)E_{n}=A_{n}(Q)-C_{n}(Q) is supported in the first and last rr block rows. Hence

rankEn≤2rd,∥En∥≤2R,∥An(Q)∥,∥Cn(Q)∥≤R.\operatorname{rank}E_{n}\leq 2rd,\qquad\|E_{n}\|\leq 2R,\qquad\|A_{n}(Q)\|,\ \|C_{n}(Q)\|\leq R.

The last bound for the Toeplitz matrix follows by compressing the Laurent operator, or directly by the triangle inequality for its partial-shift terms. Therefore

(1n​Trn​d​|En|p)1/p≤2​R​(2​r​d/n)1/p⟶0.\left(\frac{1}{n}\operatorname{Tr}_{nd}|E_{n}|^{p}\right)^{1/p}\leq 2R(2rd/n)^{1/p}\longrightarrow 0.

The discrete Fourier transform on the first tensor factor makes Cn​(Q)C_{n}(Q) block diagonal, with blocks Q⁡(ζnℓ)Q(\zeta_{n}^{\ell}), 0≤ℓ<n0\leq\ell<n, where ζn=e2​π​i/n\zeta_{n}=e^{2\pi i/n}. The triangle inequality in the Schatten pp norm scaled by n−1/pn^{-1/p} and the Riemann-sum limit prove (3.1). This uses singular values, without assuming that QQ or its Toeplitz sections are normal.

For the second assertion both matrices are Hermitian. For an integer k≥1k\geq 1, telescoping the difference of their kkth powers and using ‖En‖1≤2​R​rank⁡En\|E_{n}\|_{1}\leq 2R\operatorname{rank}E_{n} gives

1n​|Trn​d⁡(An​(Q)k−Cn​(Q)k)|≤2​k​Rk​rank⁡Enn⟶0.\frac{1}{n}\left|\operatorname{Tr}_{nd}(A_{n}(Q)^{k}-C_{n}(Q)^{k})\right|\leq\frac{2kR^{k}\operatorname{rank}E_{n}}{n}\longrightarrow 0.

The constant polynomial has equal traces on both sides. The same conclusion follows for every polynomial, and uniform polynomial approximation on the common spectral interval proves the assertion for gg. Fourier block diagonalization and the Riemann-sum limit now yield (3.2). ∎

Let SnS_{n} have ones on its first superdiagonal and zeros elsewhere. For q⁡(z)=∑k=1dαk​zkq(z)=\sum_{k=1}^{d}\alpha_{k}z^{k} put Nn=q⁡(Sn)N_{n}=q(S_{n}), which is strictly upper triangular. For real a,ba,b, set

Lemma 3.2.

Polar integration by parts gives the identity, with vanishing origin boundary terms O⁡(rp)+O⁡(rp+1)O(r^{p})+O(r^{p+1}). The radial integral ∫01rq⁡(p−2)+1​𝑑r\int_{0}^{1}r^{q(p-2)+1}\,\mathrm{d}r is finite; gradient boundary terms O⁡(εp)O(\varepsilon^{p}) make it the global weak Hessian. ∎

3.3. The homogeneous Poisson envelope

For a continuous real function GG on ℂ\mathbb{C}, let

(3.5) 𝒫(−G)(z)=infh​ holomorphic near ​𝔻¯h⁡(0)=z∫02​π−G(h(ei​t))d​t2​π.\mathcal{P}(-G)(z)=\inf_{\begin{subarray}{c}h\text{ holomorphic near }\overline{\mathbb{D}}\\ h(0)=z\end{subarray}}\int_{0}^{2\pi}-G(h(e^{it}))\frac{\,\mathrm{d}t}{2\pi}.

The Poletsky–Rosay theorem says that this function is subharmonic (possibly identically −∞-\infty) and is the largest subharmonic minorant of −G-G. The disc maps extend holomorphically past the closed unit disc; constant discs are allowed. We use the theorem on ℂ\mathbb{C} only; see [16, 17] and the formulation in [11, Section 2]. The analytic-test/majorant implication in the next lemma is also Cole’s principle [9, Theorem 2.1], applied to −G-G with the test set E={0}E=\{0\}. We include the envelope argument to specify the least majorant and the angular regularity used below.

Lemma 3.3.

Let GG be continuous and pp-homogeneous. Suppose ∫G⁡(q⁡(ei​t))​𝑑t/(2​π)≤0\int G(q(e^{it}))\,\mathrm{d}t/(2\pi)\leq 0 for every polynomial qq with q⁡(0)=0q(0)=0. Then

U∗=−𝒫⁡(−G)U_{*}=-\mathcal{P}(-G)

is a finite continuous pp-homogeneous least superharmonic majorant of GG. Its angular part is Lipschitz. It is harmonic on the open set {U∗>G}\{U_{*}>G\}.

Proof.

Taylor polynomials approximate each disc in (3.5) uniformly on 𝔻¯\overline{\mathbb{D}}, preserving its center; continuity of GG on their common compact range passes the boundary averages to the limit. Put v=𝒫⁡(−G)v=\mathcal{P}(-G). Every disc centered at zero therefore has boundary average of −G-G at least zero, and the zero disc has average zero. Hence

(3.6) v⁡(0)=0.v(0)=0.

The Poletsky–Rosay theorem therefore gives a subharmonic vv which is not identically −∞-\infty and is the largest subharmonic minorant of −G-G.

For r>0r>0, multiplication by rr is a bijection between discs centered at zz and discs centered at r​zrz. Since G⁡(r​ζ)=rp​G​(ζ)G(r\zeta)=r^{p}G(\zeta),

(3.7) v⁡(r​z)=rp​v​(z)v(rz)=r^{p}v(z)

first in the extended-real sense. We next show that no exceptional −∞-\infty values occur.

Local integrability, Fubini and (3.7) give h∈L1​(𝕋)h\in L^{1}(\mathbb{T}) with v⁡(r​ei​θ)=rp​h​(θ)v(re^{i\theta})=r^{p}h(\theta) almost everywhere. Nonnegative product tests supported in an annulus in Lemma 3.2 give

(4.9) sup|x|≤R‖h​∑|h​k|>δf⁡(x−h​k)h​k+α​h−∫|t|>δf⁡(x−t)t​𝑑t‖⟶0.\sup_{|x|\leq R}\left\|h\!\sum_{|hk|>\delta}\frac{f(x-hk)}{hk+\alpha h}-\int_{|t|>\delta}\frac{f(x-t)}{t}\,\,\mathrm{d}t\right\|\longrightarrow 0.

‖∫|t|<δf⁡(x−t)−f⁡(x)t​𝑑t‖≤CR​δ\left\|\int_{|t|<\delta}\frac{f(x-t)-f(x)}{t}\,\,\mathrm{d}t\right\|\leq C_{R}\delta

by the mean-value theorem, uniformly for |x|≤R|x|\leq R; the constant part has zero symmetric principal value. Together with the inner-sum bound above, this proves the asserted uniform convergence by first letting h↓0h\downarrow 0 with δ\delta fixed and then letting δ↓0\delta\downarrow 0.

For the joint norm estimate, set vkh=h1/p​f​(h​k)v_{k}^{h}=h^{1/p}f(hk). Then ∑k‖vkh‖pp→‖f‖Lp​(𝒮p)p\sum_{k}\|v_{k}^{h}\|_{p}^{p}\to\|f\|_{L^{p}(\mathcal{S}_{p})}^{p}. The local limit gives uniform convergence on each compact output interval for all finitely many shifts. Sum the weighted output ppth powers, pass to the Riemann integrals on that interval, and then increase the interval to ℝ\mathbb{R}. Monotone convergence gives (4.8). Smooth finite-rank functions are dense, so the estimate extends to the stated spaces.

∎

4.4. Schur realization

Lemma 4.5.

For arbitrary real pairs and nonnegative weights, supℰ‖𝐓ℰ‖=Λp​(P)\sup_{\mathcal{E}}\|\mathbf{T}_{\mathcal{E}}\|=\Lambda_{p}(P). The corresponding multiplier for the standard rank-one projections on ℓ2​(ℕ)\ell^{2}(\mathbb{N}) has the same norm.

Proof.

If X=X∗X=X^{*} and Dℰ​X=0D_{\mathcal{E}}X=0, then N=2​∑r<sEr​X​EsN=2\sum_{r<s}E_{r}XE_{s} is nilpotent with Re⁡N=X\operatorname{Re}N=X and Im⁡N=Hℰ​X\operatorname{Im}N=H_{\mathcal{E}}X. Equation (1.14) gives the joint estimate. For arbitrary zero-block-diagonal XX, Hermitian dilation and the flag Er⊗I2E_{r}\otimes I_{2} give the same bound, because every real pencil commutes with taking adjoints and all ppth powers gain a factor two.

For general XX, let u=n−1/2(1,…,1)u=n^{-1/2}(1,\ldots,1), P=u​u∗P=uu^{*}, and put

Yn=X⊗P−Dℰ​X⊗In/n,J​ξ=ξ⊗u.Y_{n}=X\otimes P-D_{\mathcal{E}}X\otimes I_{n}/n,\qquad J\xi=\xi\otimes u.

The flag ℰn=(Er⊗es​s)\mathcal{E}_{n}=(E_{r}\otimes e_{ss}), in lexicographic order, has Dℰn​Yn=0D_{\mathcal{E}_{n}}Y_{n}=0. Direct block summation gives

(4.10) J∗​Yn​J=X−Dℰ​X/n,J∗​Hℰn​(Yn)​J=Hℰ​X.J^{*}Y_{n}J=X-D_{\mathcal{E}}X/n,\qquad J^{*}H_{\mathcal{E}_{n}}(Y_{n})J=H_{\mathcal{E}}X.

The within-block signs cancel since ∑r,ssgn⁡(r−s)=0\sum_{r,s}\operatorname{sgn}(r-s)=0. Compression is contractive for each output. Summing their ppth powers and using

‖Yn−X⊗P‖p=n1/p−1​‖Dℰ​X‖p⟶0\|Y_{n}-X\otimes P\|_{p}=n^{1/p-1}\|D_{\mathcal{E}}X\|_{p}\longrightarrow 0

proves the upper bound on all XX. Conversely, Schur triangularization realizes every nilpotent as a strictly upper-triangular matrix for a rank-one flag and supplies the lower bound. Finite principal sections and density give the infinite ordered transform. ∎

4.5. Canonical amplification and trace normalization

The Schatten amplification converts the tracial matrix estimates in both parts of the paper to the usual completely bounded estimates. We record this conversion once, keeping the canonical operator-space matrix norm distinct from the tracial LpL^{p} norm.

Lemma 4.6.

Let 1<p<∞1<p<\infty, and let 𝒬,ℛ1,…,ℛm\mathcal{Q},\mathcal{R}_{1},\ldots,\mathcal{R}_{m} be semifinite tracial von Neumann algebras. Equip their LpL^{p} spaces and the finite ℓp\ell^{p} direct sum with their canonical operator-space structures. For a bounded linear map

T:Lp​(𝒬)⟶⨁j=1mLpp​(ℛj)T:L^{p}(\mathcal{Q})\longrightarrow\bigoplus_{j=1}^{m}{}_{\!p}L^{p}(\mathcal{R}_{j})

one has

(4.11) ‖T‖cb=supn≥1‖idMn⊗T‖tr,\|T\|_{\mathrm{cb}}=\sup_{n\geq 1}\|\operatorname{id}_{M_{n}}\otimes T\|_{\mathrm{tr}},

where the norm on the right is between the corresponding tracial spaces

Lp​(Mn​⊗¯​𝒬)and⨁j=1mLpp​(Mn​⊗¯​ℛj).L^{p}(M_{n}\,\overline{\otimes}\,\mathcal{Q})\quad\hbox{and}\quad\bigoplus_{j=1}^{m}{}_{\!p}L^{p}(M_{n}\,\overline{\otimes}\,\mathcal{R}_{j}).

The matrix trace in these spaces is the ordinary unnormalized trace. Replacing it simultaneously in the domain and range by n−1​Trnn^{-1}\operatorname{Tr}_{n} does not change any amplification norm.

Proof.

The standard Schatten Fubini identification and matrix-norm recovery formula are

(4.12) 𝒮pn​[Lp​(𝒬)]\displaystyle\mathcal{S}_{p}^{n}[L^{p}(\mathcal{Q})] =Lp​(Mn​⊗¯​𝒬),\displaystyle=L^{p}(M_{n}\,\overline{\otimes}\,\mathcal{Q}),
(4.13) ‖x‖Mn​(Lp​(𝒬))\displaystyle\|x\|_{M_{n}(L^{p}(\mathcal{Q}))} =supa,b∈Mn‖a‖𝒮2​pn,‖b‖𝒮2​pn≤1‖(a⊗I)​x​(b⊗I)‖Lp​(Mn​⊗¯​𝒬).\displaystyle=\sup_{\begin{subarray}{c}a,b\in M_{n}\\ \|a\|_{\mathcal{S}_{2p}^{n}},\,\|b\|_{\mathcal{S}_{2p}^{n}}\leq 1\end{subarray}}\|(a\otimes I)x(b\otimes I)\|_{L^{p}(M_{n}\,\overline{\otimes}\,\mathcal{Q})}.

Here the Schatten norms are unnormalized. These identities, and the equivalence of complete contraction with contraction at every Schatten pp-amplification, are recalled in [35, Section 2, equations (2.8)–(2.9)]; see also [19, Corollary 1.4 and Lemma 1.7]. The range is the LpL^{p} space of the finite direct-sum algebra ⨁jℛj\bigoplus_{j}\mathcal{R}_{j}, with the direct-sum trace, so the same identifications apply there.

For completeness, if all tracial amplification norms are at most CC, entrywise amplification commutes with multiplication by the scalar matrices a,ba,b. Formula (4.13) therefore gives

‖(idMn⊗T)​x‖Mn​(F)≤C​‖x‖Mn​(Lp​(𝒬)),F=⨁j=1mLpp​(ℛj).\|(\operatorname{id}_{M_{n}}\otimes T)x\|_{M_{n}(F)}\leq C\|x\|_{M_{n}(L^{p}(\mathcal{Q}))},\qquad F=\bigoplus_{j=1}^{m}{}_{\!p}L^{p}(\mathcal{R}_{j}).

Thus ‖T‖cb≤C\|T\|_{\mathrm{cb}}\leq C. Conversely, the standard Schatten amplification characterization bounds every id𝒮pn⊗T\operatorname{id}_{\mathcal{S}_{p}^{n}}\otimes T by ‖T‖cb\|T\|_{\mathrm{cb}}; (4.12) identifies its norm with the tracial amplification norm. This proves (4.11). Normalizing the matrix trace multiplies both the domain and range norms by n−1/pn^{-1/p}, proving the final assertion. ∎

In particular, a uniform estimate for the amplified flags in the Hilbert part and a uniform estimate for Mn​(ℬ)⊂Mn​(ℳ)M_{n}(\mathcal{B})\subset M_{n}(\mathcal{M}) in the subdiagonal part give the corresponding completely bounded estimates by the same lemma. The sharp tracial estimates themselves are proved separately in the two parts.

In the present cases the Fubini identifications for vector-valued noncommutative LpL^{p} spaces are

(4.14) 𝒮pd​[Lp​(ℝ)]=Lp​(ℝ,𝒮pd),𝒮pd​[𝒮p​(ℓ2)]=𝒮p​(ℂd⊗ℓ2).\mathcal{S}_{p}^{d}[L^{p}(\mathbb{R})]=L^{p}(\mathbb{R};\mathcal{S}_{p}^{d}),\qquad\mathcal{S}_{p}^{d}[\mathcal{S}_{p}(\ell^{2})]=\mathcal{S}_{p}(\mathbb{C}^{d}\otimes\ell^{2}).

The norms in the right-hand spaces use the unnormalized trace, consistently with the rest of the paper. Formula (4.11) compares the corresponding amplification norms of a map.

Proof of Theorem 1.4.

Lemma 4.1 gives finiteness, and Corollary 3.7 gives the variational and superharmonic majorant statements. For the shifted pairs, scalar embedding, sampling, finite-window transference, and the same lemma give the following chain of inequalities:

(4.15) ‖𝐇‖scalar≤‖𝐇‖𝒮p≤‖𝐑‖𝒮p≤Λp​(P)≤‖𝐇‖scalar.\|\mathbf{H}\|_{\rm scalar}\leq\|\mathbf{H}\|_{\mathcal{S}_{p}}\leq\|\mathbf{R}\|_{\mathcal{S}_{p}}\leq\Lambda_{p}(P)\leq\|\mathbf{H}\|_{\rm scalar}.

Applying sampling also with 𝒦=ℂ\mathcal{K}=\mathbb{C} and embedding scalar sequences shows ‖𝐑‖scalar=Λp​(P)\|\mathbf{R}\|_{\rm scalar}=\Lambda_{p}(P). Lemma 4.5 supplies the Schur model.

For general pairs with bj≠0b_{j}\neq 0, multiplying an output by −1-1 if necessary permits the representation (aj,bj)=εj​rj​(cos⁡(π​αj),sin⁡(π​αj))(a_{j},b_{j})=\varepsilon_{j}r_{j}(\cos(\pi\alpha_{j}),\sin(\pi\alpha_{j})), where εj∈{−1,1}\varepsilon_{j}\in\{-1,1\}, rj>0r_{j}>0, and 0<αj<10<\alpha_{j}<1. Absorb rjpr_{j}^{p} into wjw_{j}. The outputs with bj=0b_{j}=0 add the same constant ∑bj=0wj​|aj|p\sum_{b_{j}=0}w_{j}|a_{j}|^{p} to every norm ratio to the ppth power, including the nilpotent and disc ratios. This proves all real pairs, including the case of zero weights. Finally tr⁡N2=0\operatorname{tr}N^{2}=0 gives tr⁡A2=tr⁡B2\operatorname{tr}A^{2}=\operatorname{tr}B^{2} and tr⁡A​B=0\operatorname{tr}AB=0, which proves the stated quadratic value.

For completely bounded norms, the same Fubini identifications hold for ℓp​(ℤ)\ell^{p}(\mathbb{Z}) and finite ℓp\ell^{p} direct sums. Thus the ddth Schatten amplification of 𝐇\mathbf{H} or 𝐑\mathbf{R} is exactly its 𝒮pd\mathcal{S}_{p}^{d}-valued version, whose norm is Λp​(P)\Lambda_{p}(P). The ddth amplification of 𝐓ℰ\mathbf{T}_{\mathcal{E}} is the same joint pencil for the block flag (Id⊗Ej)(I_{d}\otimes E_{j}), up to interchange of tensor factors. Hence its norm is at most Λp​(P)\Lambda_{p}(P), uniformly in dd and the flag. Taking the supremum in the amplification characterization and using the operator-norm lower bounds proves the completely bounded norm assertions of the theorem.

For the standard infinite Schur order, finite principal sections and density at every amplification level give the same upper bound; nilpotent tests on rank-one flags give the lower bound. ∎

Proof of Corollary 1.5.

For one output, the scalar theorem of [9, 10] gives (1.18). Theorem 1.4 and the preceding infinite-order argument give every stated norm equality. Scalar reflection, homogeneity, and duality give (1.19)–(1.20). Only the signed diagonal convention remains, and it is proved next. ∎

Corollary 4.7.

Use the real pairs and weights of Theorem 1.4. For real row levels λ1,…,λr\lambda_{1},\ldots,\lambda_{r} and column levels μ1,…,μs\mu_{1},\ldots,\mu_{s}, define the joint rectangular multiplier

(𝐌λ,μ​X)ℓ=(wℓ1/p​[aℓ+i​bℓ​sgn⁡(λj−μk)]​Xj​k)j,k.(\mathbf{M}_{\lambda,\mu}X)_{\ell}=\bigl(w_{\ell}^{1/p}[a_{\ell}+ib_{\ell}\operatorname{sgn}(\lambda_{j}-\mu_{k})]X_{jk}\bigr)_{j,k}.

On rectangular Schatten matrices with their canonical corner operator-space structure, it is the restriction of a single joint flag multiplier on ℂr+s\mathbb{C}^{r+s} to a rectangular corner, under a complete isometry. Hence its operator and completely bounded norms are at most Λp​(P)\Lambda_{p}(P), and their suprema over all finite lists and sizes equal Λp​(P)\Lambda_{p}(P). For one output this gives the bound and uniform sharp constant Kp​(a,b)K_{p}(a,b).

Proof.

Embed XX in the off-diagonal corner from the μ\mu-space to the λ\lambda-space of their direct sum, and order the combined levels, grouping ties. This embedding preserves singular values at every Schatten amplification and is completely isometric by (4.13). The resulting joint flag preserves the corner and has exactly the displayed symbols. Theorem 1.4 gives both upper bounds. Equal square lists recover the standard rank-one joint orders; their uniform sharpness in Lemma 4.5 gives both lower bounds. ∎

when SS acts on n×nn\times n matrices. Then

Lemma 5.5.

For bounded A,B≥0A,B\geq 0,

We give a direct proof of the relevant rearrangement inequality; see [28] for its general formulation. For A≥0A\geq 0 and 0≤q≤10\leq q\leq 1, the Ky Fan formula is

∫0qμv(A)dv=sup{τ(AQ):0≤Q≤I,τQ=q}.\int_{0}^{q}\mu_{v}(A)\,dv=\sup\{\tau(AQ):0\leq Q\leq I,\ \tau Q=q\}.

6. Analytic witnesses and the sharp Riesz theorem

We construct analytic test elements whose pairing with the retained summand is exact. For 2<p<42<p<4, factorization converts determinant covariance into an L2L^{2} angle estimate. For p>4p>4, the positive canonical estimate supplies the test element directly. The analytic regularization behind that estimate is proved in Appendix D without sharp boundedness. Continuity and duality complete the retained projection; a subdiagonal corner construction then gives the strict projection.

Corollary 5.10 and analytic factorization supply this interval without any previously established sharp projection estimate.

For 1<p<21<p<2 let q=p′>2q=p^{\prime}>2. The preceding arguments bound PP on LqL^{q}. On 𝒞\mathcal{C} the trace adjoint of PP is itself by (C.1). The strict projection and uniform sharpness

In M2​(ℳ)M_{2}(\mathcal{M}), with normalized matrix trace, consider

ℬ~=(ℬℬ0ℬℬ),Φ~​(xyzw)=(Φ​x00Φ​w).\widetilde{\mathcal{B}}=\begin{pmatrix}\mathcal{B}&\mathcal{B}_{0}\\ \mathcal{B}&\mathcal{B}\end{pmatrix},\qquad\widetilde{\Phi}\begin{pmatrix}x&y\\ z&w\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}\Phi x&0\\ 0&\Phi w\end{pmatrix}.

Take ℳ=L∞​(𝕋)\mathcal{M}=L^{\infty}(\mathbb{T}) with normalized Haar trace and ℬ=H∞​(𝕋)\mathcal{B}=H^{\infty}(\mathbb{T}). For 0<b<1/p0<b<1/p put

hb​(z)=(1+z1−z)b,cb=cos⁡(π​b).h_{b}(z)=\left(\frac{1+z}{1-z}\right)^{b},\qquad c_{b}=\cos(\pi b).

The principal power is analytic in the disk and hb​(0)=1h_{b}(0)=1. Its boundary values have modulus |cot⁡(t/2)|b|\cot(t/2)|^{b} and argument ±πb/2\pm\pi b/2. Hence, pointwise almost everywhere,

|hb−cb​hb¯|=sin⁡(π​b)​|hb|.|h_{b}-c_{b}\overline{h_{b}}|=\sin(\pi b)|h_{b}|.

Optimality of the coefficient in Theorem 1.2.

Fix 0<β<10<\beta<1 and put p=2​(1+β)p=2(1+\beta), so that the squared coefficient in (1.3) is cos2⁡(π/p)\cos^{2}(\pi/p). 7. Weighted angular realization and cone duality

Tracial joint spectral measures need not have finite total mass. Indeed, for a nonzero nilpotent matrix NN, one has A=Re⁡N≠0A=\operatorname{Re}N\neq 0, and

∫|x|q​d​μA,B=tr⁡|A|qq⁡(q+1)⟶∞(q↓0).\int|x|^{q}\,\mathrm{d}\mu_{A,B}=\frac{\operatorname{tr}|A|^{q}}{q(q+1)}\longrightarrow\infty\quad(q\downarrow 0).

The compact support shows that a finite total mass would contradict this divergence. We therefore use finite weighted pushforward measures on the circle. Throughout this section, C⁡(𝕋)C(\mathbb{T}) denotes the real-valued continuous functions on 𝕋\mathbb{T}.

Definition 7.1.

For a nilpotent N=A+i​BN=A+iB, define the finite positive measure νN\nu_{N} on 𝕋\mathbb{T} by

For a polynomial qq with q⁡(0)=0q(0)=0, define

(7.2) ∫𝕋g​d​σq=∫02​π|q⁡(ei​t)|p​g​(arg⁡q⁡(ei​t))​d​t2​π,\int_{\mathbb{T}}g\,\mathrm{d}\sigma_{q}=\int_{0}^{2\pi}|q(e^{it})|^{p}g(\arg q(e^{it}))\frac{\,\mathrm{d}t}{2\pi},

with integrand zero when q⁡(ei​t)=0q(e^{it})=0. Put

𝒮p={u∈C⁡(𝕋):ℒp​u:=u′′+p2​u≤0​ distributionally},\mathscr{S}_{p}=\{u\in C(\mathbb{T}):\ \mathcal{L}_{p}u:=u^{\prime\prime}+p^{2}u\leq 0\text{ distributionally}\},

(7.3) 𝒥p={ν≥0:∫u​𝑑ν≤0​ for every ​u∈𝒮p}.\mathscr{J}_{p}=\{\nu\geq 0:\ \int u\,\mathrm{d}\nu\leq 0\text{ for every }u\in\mathscr{S}_{p}\}.
Theorem 7.2.

In the weak-* topology of finite measures paired with C⁡(𝕋)C(\mathbb{T}),

(7.4) cone⁡{νN:N​ finite nilpotent}¯w∗=cone⁡{σq:q⁡(0)=0}¯w∗=𝒥p.\overline{\operatorname{cone}\{\nu_{N}:N\text{ finite nilpotent}\}}^{\,w^{*}}=\overline{\operatorname{cone}\{\sigma_{q}:q(0)=0\}}^{\,w^{*}}=\mathscr{J}_{p}.

(7.5) 1n​νq⁡(Sn)⟶σqweak-*.\frac{1}{n}\nu_{q(S_{n})}\longrightarrow\sigma_{q}\qquad\text{weak-*}.

(7.6) 𝒥p={ν≥0:ν=ℒpω,ω∈C(𝕋),ω≥0}.\mathscr{J}_{p}=\{\nu\geq 0:\ \nu=\mathcal{L}_{p}\omega,\quad\omega\in C(\mathbb{T}),\quad\omega\geq 0\}.

Proof.

We first prove the approximation assertion for continuous angular tests. Put Nn=q⁡(Sn)=An+i​BnN_{n}=q(S_{n})=A_{n}+iB_{n}, μn=n−1​μAn,Bn\mu_{n}=n^{-1}\mu_{A_{n},B_{n}}, and ηn=|z|2​μn\eta_{n}=|z|^{2}\mu_{n}. Their supports lie in a common compact square. Define the finite measure

The first inclusion is (7.5). For a finite nilpotent define

(7.9) ωN(p)​(θ)=12​π​∫0∞ΨN​(r​ei​θ)​rp−1​𝑑r≥0.\omega_{N}^{(p)}(\theta)=\frac{1}{2\pi}\int_{0}^{\infty}\Psi_{N}(re^{i\theta})r^{p-1}\,\mathrm{d}r\geq 0.

If ω∈L1​(𝕋)\omega\in L^{1}(\mathbb{T}) is nonnegative and ℒp​ω=ν≥0\mathcal{L}_{p}\omega=\nu\geq 0, testing against 11 gives p2​∫ω​𝑑θ=m=ν⁡(𝕋)p^{2}\int\omega\,\mathrm{d}\theta=m=\nu(\mathbb{T}). Finally let KkK_{k} be the nonnegative Fejér kernels normalized by ∫Kk​𝑑θ=1\int K_{k}\,\mathrm{d}\theta=1. Put ωk=Kk∗ω\omega_{k}=K_{k}*\omega and vk=Kk∗νv_{k}=K_{k}*\nu. Positivity, the mass identity, and vk=ℒp​ωkv_{k}=\mathcal{L}_{p}\omega_{k} are preserved; the asserted convergences are the approximate-identity properties. At an integer exponent p≥2p\geq 2, every ν∈𝒥p\nu\in\mathscr{J}_{p} satisfies ∫𝕋ei​p​θ​𝑑ν​(θ)=0\int_{\mathbb{T}}e^{ip\theta}\,\,\mathrm{d}\nu(\theta)=0, since both signs of cos⁡(p​θ)\cos(p\theta) and sin⁡(p​θ)\sin(p\theta) belong to 𝒮p\mathscr{S}_{p}. Any two potentials for the same measure differ by a​cos⁡(p​θ)+b​sin⁡(p​θ)a\cos(p\theta)+b\sin(p\theta), with a,b∈ℝa,b\in\mathbb{R}. The bounds above hold for every nonnegative potential, so no normalization of this kernel component is needed in the compactness argument. ∎

8. Sharp consequences

We first pass the finite trace certificate to compact operators and obtain the exact comparison for a prescribed spectral set, followed by its real diagonal perturbation consequence. At exponent four, the directional moment disk gives an explicit signed classification and joint norm formula. We then realize the analytic-distance theorem as sharp triangular and Fourier projection bounds.

8.1. Compact spectral corrections

Compressing a quasinilpotent operator need not preserve quasinilpotence. The spectral correction must be passed to the limit.

Theorem 8.1.

Let 1<p<∞1<p<\infty and Tn→TT_{n}\to T in 𝒮p\mathcal{S}_{p}, with all operators compact. List their nonzero eigenvalues with algebraic multiplicities and append countably many zeros. For two such lists define

dp​(Λ⁡(S),Λ⁡(T))=infσ(∑j≥1|λj​(S)−λσ⁡(j)​(T)|p)1/p,d_{p}(\Lambda(S),\Lambda(T))=\inf_{\sigma}\left(\sum_{j\geq 1}|\lambda_{j}(S)-\lambda_{\sigma(j)}(T)|^{p}\right)^{1/p},

(8.1) bδ​(S):=(∑0<|λj​(S)|≤δ|λj​(S)|p)1/p≤‖S−F‖p+δ1/p′​‖F‖11/p.b_{\delta}(S):=\left(\sum_{0<|\lambda_{j}(S)|\leq\delta}|\lambda_{j}(S)|^{p}\right)^{1/p}\leq\|S-F\|_{p}+\delta^{1/p^{\prime}}\|F\|_{1}^{1/p}.

For every κ∈ℝ\kappa\in\mathbb{R},

Put K=max⁡{Cp,maxj⁡|κj|}K=\max\{C_{p},\max_{j}|\kappa_{j}|\}. For X=X∗X=X^{*}, set Y=Hℰ​X+∑jκj​Ej​X​EjY=H_{\mathcal{E}}X+\sum_{j}\kappa_{j}E_{j}XE_{j}. The block upper-triangular matrix i⁡(X+i​Y)=−Y+i​Xi(X+iY)=-Y+iX has diagonal blocks (−κj+i)​Ej​X​Ej(-\kappa_{j}+i)E_{j}XE_{j}, so its spectrum lies in Σp,K\Sigma_{p,K}. For a bounded sequence 𝜿\boldsymbol{\kappa}, the diagonal series converges in 𝒮p\mathcal{S}_{p} and contractivity of DD gives ‖D𝜿​X‖p≤‖𝜿‖∞​‖X‖p\|D_{\boldsymbol{\kappa}}X\|_{p}\leq\|\boldsymbol{\kappa}\|_{\infty}\|X\|_{p}. This real diagonal perturbation preserves self-adjointness. The signed conventions S0±DS_{0}\pm D from Lemma 4.8 instead become Hℰ±i​DℰH_{\mathcal{E}}\pm iD_{\mathcal{E}} after multiplication by ii; their normalization comparison is a separate assertion.

8.3. Fourth-power moment geometry

Theorem 8.5.

For every nonzero finite nilpotent N=A+i​BN=A+iB, its directional fourth moments have the form

(8.11) tr⁡|A​cos⁡θ+B​sin⁡θ|4=M⁡(1+u​cos⁡2​θ+v​sin⁡2​θ),M>0.\operatorname{tr}|A\cos\theta+B\sin\theta|^{4}=M(1+u\cos 2\theta+v\sin 2\theta),\qquad M>0.

With ρ=2​2/3\rho=2\sqrt{2}/3, the closure of all these normalized moment pairs is precisely {(u,v):u2+v2≤ρ2}\{(u,v):u^{2}+v^{2}\leq\rho^{2}\}. For arbitrary real a,ba,b, homogeneity gives

(8.12) 1M​tr⁡|a​A+b​B|4=(a2+b2)2+(a2+b2)​[(a2−b2)​u+2​a​b​v].\frac{1}{M}\operatorname{tr}|aA+bB|^{4}=(a^{2}+b^{2})^{2}+(a^{2}+b^{2})[(a^{2}-b^{2})u+2abv].
Proof.

For nonzero nilpotent N=A+i​BN=A+iB, write EN​(θ)=tr⁡|A​cos⁡θ+B​sin⁡θ|4E_{N}(\theta)=\operatorname{tr}|A\cos\theta+B\sin\theta|^{4}. Expanding via A​cos⁡θ+B​sin⁡θ=(e−i​θ​N+ei​θ​N∗)/2A\cos\theta+B\sin\theta=(e^{-i\theta}N+e^{i\theta}N^{*})/2, the fourth harmonics vanish because tr⁡N4=0\operatorname{tr}N^{4}=0. Thus, for some M>0M>0,

EN​(θ)=M⁡(1+u​cos⁡2​θ+v​sin⁡2​θ).E_{N}(\theta)=M(1+u\cos 2\theta+v\sin 2\theta).

Every directional part A​cos⁡θ+B​sin⁡θA\cos\theta+B\sin\theta is nonzero: otherwise a rotation of NN would be skew-Hermitian and nilpotent, hence zero. Thus r=(u2+v2)1/2<1r=(u^{2}+v^{2})^{1/2}<1. Apply the sharp coordinate inequality to every rotation of NN. The maximum ratio of orthogonal directional fourth moments is (1+r)/(1−r)(1+r)/(1-r), whence

r≤C44−1C44+1=2​23=:ρ.r\leq\frac{C_{4}^{4}-1}{C_{4}^{4}+1}=\frac{2\sqrt{2}}{3}=:\rho.

Conversely sharpness of C4=1+2C_{4}=1+\sqrt{2} among finite nilpotents gives a sequence of moment pairs (u,v)(u,v) approaching the boundary circle. Rotating the nilpotents realizes every boundary direction in the closure. Direct sums, with positive fourth-power rescaling, take convex combinations of these moment pairs. Their closure is therefore exactly the disk u2+v2≤ρ2u^{2}+v^{2}\leq\rho^{2}.

∎

8.4. A complete fourth-power criterion

The moment disk turns the signed classification at p=4p=4 into an explicit second-order cone condition.

For finitely many real cj,aj,bjc_{j},a_{j},b_{j}, put

Γ0\displaystyle\Gamma_{0} =∑jcj​(aj2+bj2)2,\displaystyle=\sum_{j}c_{j}(a_{j}^{2}+b_{j}^{2})^{2},

if and only if

(8.15) Γ0+2​23​Γ12+Γ22≤0.\Gamma_{0}+\frac{2\sqrt{2}}{3}\sqrt{\Gamma_{1}^{2}+\Gamma_{2}^{2}}\leq 0.

Equivalently, the coefficient triple belongs to a scaled negative Lorentz cone. This criterion also characterizes the existence of an admissible superharmonic majorant of ∑jcj​|aj​x+bj​y|4\sum_{j}c_{j}|a_{j}x+b_{j}y|^{4}, and the inequality then holds for every compact quasinilpotent A+i​B∈𝒮4A+iB\in\mathcal{S}_{4}.

For N=A+i​B≠0N=A+iB\neq 0, use the normalization (8.11). Theorem 8.5 gives the closed moment disk u2+v2≤8/9u^{2}+v^{2}\leq 8/9. Summing the directional fourth moments with their signed coefficients gives

1M​∑jcj​tr⁡|aj​A+bj​B|4=Γ0+Γ1​u+Γ2​v.\frac{1}{M}\sum_{j}c_{j}\operatorname{tr}|a_{j}A+b_{j}B|^{4}=\Gamma_{0}+\Gamma_{1}u+\Gamma_{2}v.

The supremum over the closed disk is the left side of (8.15). If it is positive, a nearby realized moment pair gives a finite nilpotent counterexample; if it is nonpositive, every pair satisfies (8.14). The zero matrix is immediate. Theorem 1.3 and Corollary 8.3 give the majorant and compact-operator assertions. ∎

The coordinate value C4C_{4} used in this derivation is classical [18, Theorem 6.2]. The corollary makes the entire signed fourth-power classification explicit; it requires no additional estimate beyond the moment disk.

Let P,QP,Q be finite signed fourth-power ridge sums, with coefficient triples (Γ0,Γ1,Γ2)(\Gamma_{0},\Gamma_{1},\Gamma_{2}) and (Q0,Q1,Q2)(Q_{0},Q_{1},Q_{2}) as in (8.13). Assume Q0>ρ​Q12+Q22Q_{0}>\rho\sqrt{Q_{1}^{2}+Q_{2}^{2}}, and put

a\displaystyle a =Q02−ρ2​(Q12+Q22),\displaystyle=Q_{0}^{2}-\rho^{2}(Q_{1}^{2}+Q_{2}^{2}),

Proof.

The hypothesis is exactly positivity of the denominator on the closed moment disk. Corollary 8.6, applied to P−λ​QP-\lambda Q, gives (8.17); its left side minus its right side is strictly increasing from −∞-\infty to +∞+\infty. The compact assertion follows from Corollary 8.6; nonnegative ridge coefficients give Q0>0Q_{0}>0 and Q12+Q22≤Q0\sqrt{Q_{1}^{2}+Q_{2}^{2}}\leq Q_{0}, proving the final assertion. ∎

(8.18) Λ4​(P)4=A0+17​B0+4​2​9​B02+C02.\Lambda_{4}(P)^{4}=A_{0}+17B_{0}+4\sqrt{2}\sqrt{9B_{0}^{2}+C_{0}^{2}}.

(8.21) K4​(a,b)2=K4/3​(a,b)2=a2+b2​(a2+9​b2+2​2​|b|).K_{4}(a,b)^{2}=K_{4/3}(a,b)^{2}=\sqrt{a^{2}+b^{2}}\left(\sqrt{a^{2}+9b^{2}}+2\sqrt{2}\,|b|\right).

(8.22) ‖Rα‖2=1+8​sin2⁡(π​α)+2​2​sin⁡(π​α).\|R_{\alpha}\|^{2}=\sqrt{1+8\sin^{2}(\pi\alpha)}+2\sqrt{2}\sin(\pi\alpha).

Every nonzero vector has first coordinate positive. Equality in the Euclidean triangle inequality holds exactly when these vectors are positively collinear, equivalently when their ratios Cj/Bj=aj/bjC_{j}/B_{j}=a_{j}/b_{j} agree. For shifted pairs, A0=(W+Re⁡Z)/2A_{0}=(W+\operatorname{Re}Z)/2, B0=(W−Re⁡Z)/2B_{0}=(W-\operatorname{Re}Z)/2, C0=Im⁡Z/2C_{0}=\operatorname{Im}Z/2, which proves (8.20). For several pencils, the adjoint maps an ℓp′\ell^{p^{\prime}} direct sum into a single space, so it does not give the same joint norm identity at p′p^{\prime}. ∎

For example, two unit-weight shifts α1=1/4\alpha_{1}=1/4, α2=3/4\alpha_{2}=3/4 give

The compatibility condition concerns common approximate extremizers. Indeed, a sequence saturating the joint sum must saturate every positive-weight summand; conversely proportional nonidentity pencils share a single-pencil extremizing sequence.

Comparisons of arbitrary real directions and products of joint families acting in independent coordinates are recorded in Appendix E.

Remark 8.9.

The planar majorant applies to real linear combinations a​A+b​BaA+bB of self-adjoint operators. The norm formula does not extend to arbitrary complex coefficients a,ba,b. For example, on 𝒮2\mathcal{S}_{2} let X=e12X=e_{12}. Then Hℰ​X=−i​XH_{\mathcal{E}}X=-iX, so ‖(I+i​Hℰ)​X‖2=2​‖X‖2\|(I+iH_{\mathcal{E}})X\|_{2}=2\|X\|_{2}. Substituting (a,b)=(1,i)(a,b)=(1,i) in the absolute-value angular ratio in (1.18) instead gives 2\sqrt{2} at p=2p=2. This explicit failure rules out that complex extension. In particular, the sharp real-combination results, including the completely bounded equalities of Corollary 1.5, do not establish a sharp Riesz or triangular projection bound.

8.6. Riesz projections and matrix amplification

We apply Theorem 1.1 to matrix and Fourier realizations. The amplification bound is used at every matrix level before it is converted to a canonical completely bounded estimate.

Corollary 8.10.

For every algebra in Theorem 1.1, every 1<p<∞1<p<\infty, and every n≥1n\geq 1,

‖IdMn⊗P‖Lp​(Mn​⊗¯​ℳ)→Lp​(Mn​⊗¯​ℳ),‖IdMn⊗P0‖Lp​(Mn​⊗¯​ℳ)→Lp​(Mn​⊗¯​ℳ)≤csc⁡(π/p).\|\operatorname{Id}_{M_{n}}\otimes P\|_{L^{p}(M_{n}\overline{\otimes}\mathcal{M})\to L^{p}(M_{n}\overline{\otimes}\mathcal{M})},\quad\|\operatorname{Id}_{M_{n}}\otimes P_{0}\|_{L^{p}(M_{n}\overline{\otimes}\mathcal{M})\to L^{p}(M_{n}\overline{\otimes}\mathcal{M})}\leq\csc(\pi/p).

For the canonical operator space structure on Lp​(ℳ)L^{p}(\mathcal{M}), also

‖P‖cb,‖P0‖cb≤csc⁡(π/p).\|P\|_{\mathrm{cb}},\ \|P_{0}\|_{\mathrm{cb}}\leq\csc(\pi/p).

These are uniform upper bounds; a particular subdiagonal algebra need not attain them.

Proof.

The algebra Mn​(ℬ)M_{n}(\mathcal{B}) is subdiagonal in Mn​(ℳ)M_{n}(\mathcal{M}), with diagonal Mn​(𝒟)M_{n}(\mathcal{D}) and expectation IdMn⊗Φ\operatorname{Id}_{M_{n}}\otimes\Phi. Multiplicativity, trace preservation, and weak-star density hold entrywise; Theorem C.1(3) gives maximality. Its retained and strict projections are the stated amplifications, so Theorem 1.1 proves the tracial bounds. The normalized matrix trace may be replaced by the ordinary trace, since this scales both norms by the same factor.

Lemma 4.6 now converts these uniform tracial amplification bounds to the stated canonical completely bounded bounds. This application uses no additional sharp estimate and keeps the tracial and operator-space matrix norms distinct. ∎

For n≥1n\geq 1, let Tn((xi​j))=(1{i≤j}xi​j)T_{n}((x_{ij}))=(1_{\{i\leq j\}}x_{ij}) be retained-diagonal upper triangular truncation; SnpS_{n}^{p} denotes the Schatten pp-class on ℂn\mathbb{C}^{n}.

Let 1<p<∞1<p<\infty and let (ℳ,τ)(\mathcal{M},\tau) be any finite von Neumann algebra with a faithful normal tracial state. Then

Remark 8.12.

This corollary is the exact infinite-size norm of triangular truncation, including finite-algebra coefficients. The Fourier–Schur transference relation proved by Neuwirth and Ricard [18, Proposition 6.3] places it in the corresponding completely bounded scalar Fourier-multiplier framework; the proof here does not require that transference result.

9. Limitations of the two-point criterion

The scalar two-term pencil is governed by an angular quotient involving two points separated by π/p\pi/p. For a general homogeneous obstacle, consider the necessary conditions

(9.1) f⁡(θ)+f⁡(θ+π/p)≤0for every ​θ.f(\theta)+f(\theta+\pi/p)\leq 0\qquad\text{for every }\theta.

These tests are necessary: extend sin⁡(p⁡(θ−α))\sin(p(\theta-\alpha)) on [α,α+π/p][\alpha,\alpha+\pi/p] by zero periodically. It is nonnegative and its ℒp\mathcal{L}_{p} is p⁡(δα+δα+π/p)p(\delta_{\alpha}+\delta_{\alpha+\pi/p}); pairing with a superharmonic angular majorant proves (9.1). They are not sufficient for general finite real ridge sums. The two-point criterion of [9, Theorem 3.7] requires additional sector hypotheses on the homogeneous obstacle. The example below shows why such restrictions cannot be dropped in the present class.

In both cases |arg⁡z|≤π/(2​p)|\arg z|\leq\pi/(2p) and |(p−2)​arg⁡z|<π/2|(p-2)\arg z|<\pi/2, so the derivative is nonpositive. The established C1C^{1} and Sobolev regularity excludes singular interface terms. For t=K/Cp≥1t=K/C_{p}\geq 1, almost everywhere,

Δ⁡[Up​(x,t​y)]=(Δ​Up)​(x,t​y)+(t2−1)​(∂y2Up)​(x,t​y)≤0.\Delta[U_{p}(x,ty)]=(\Delta U_{p})(x,ty)+(t^{2}-1)(\partial_{y}^{2}U_{p})(x,ty)\leq 0.

Linear change of variables preserves the regularity, and the majorization and sign assertions follow directly from those of UpU_{p}. ∎

Consequently (8.7) has exactly the two remainder terms in (2.23), with no further operator argument. Its spectral correction can be dropped when spec⁡T⊂Σp\operatorname{spec}T\subset\Sigma_{p}, or whenever the signed eigenvalue sum is nonpositive. The Laplacian vanishes on a full sector, so positivity of ΨT\Psi_{T} alone gives no uniform stability lower bound.

Appendix B Weyl comparison and normalization

The spectral transfer theorem in Section 2 also identifies a compactly supported Weyl distribution and quantifies its difference from the eigenvalue measure. We record those consequences and the normalizations used in their potential-theoretic interpretation.

Example B.1.

For scalar T=a+i​bT=a+ib one can take μa,b=∫01(1−r)​r−1​δ(r​a,r​b)​𝑑r\mu_{a,b}=\int_{0}^{1}(1-r)r^{-1}\delta_{(ra,rb)}\,\mathrm{d}r on ℝ2∖{0}\mathbb{R}^{2}\setminus\{0\}. Its positive radial moments are finite, whereas its mass is infinite if (a,b)≠(0,0)(a,b)\neq(0,0). For T=1T=1, reflection of this measure preserves every absolute directional moment but changes ∫x​𝑑μ\int x\,\mathrm{d}\mu from 1/21/2 to −1/2-1/2. Thus the full ridge identity, not just power moments, is necessary.

The distribution below is the scalar trace of Anderson’s Weyl functional calculus [4, 5], characterized by its Fourier transform tr⁡ei⁡(ξ1​A+ξ2​B)\operatorname{tr}e^{i(\xi_{1}A+\xi_{2}B)}. Its relation to tracial joint spectral measures is discussed in [3, Sections 0.1.1–0.1.3]. The corollary records its radial reconstruction from μA,B\mu_{A,B} and its comparison with the eigenvalue measure through ΨT\Psi_{T}.

Remark B.6.

For this comparison only, normalize the trace by τ=d−1​tr\tau=d^{-1}\operatorname{tr}. The Fuglede–Kadison determinant [6] of an invertible matrix SS is Detτ⁡(S)=exp⁡τ⁡(log⁡|S|)=|detS|1/d\operatorname{Det}_{\tau}(S)=\exp\tau(\log|S|)=|\det S|^{1/d}. The Brown measure of TT [7] is the normalized eigenvalue measure νTB=d−1​∑jδλj​(T)\nu_{T}^{\mathrm{B}}=d^{-1}\sum_{j}\delta_{\lambda_{j}(T)}. For w∉spec⁡Tw\notin\operatorname{spec}T,

log⁡Detτ⁡(T−w​I)=∫log⁡|w−z|​d​νTB​(z).\log\operatorname{Det}_{\tau}(T-wI)=\int\log|w-z|\,\mathrm{d}\nu_{T}^{\mathrm{B}}(z).

By (B.3), the normalized defect satisfies

(B.8) 1dΨT=(log|⋅|)∗(1d𝔚T−νTB)≥0almost everywhere.\frac{1}{d}\Psi_{T}=(\log|\cdot|)*\left(\frac{1}{d}\mathfrak{W}_{T}-\nu_{T}^{\mathrm{B}}\right)\geq 0\quad\text{almost everywhere}.

Thus the logarithmic potential of the trace Weyl distribution dominates that of the Brown measure, although the Weyl distribution itself can fail positivity. This gives an operator-algebraic interpretation of the finite-dimensional spectral defect. Matsaev–Sodin already pointed to Brown’s determinant theory as a setting for extensions of spectral inequalities [24]. Extending this real-directional mechanism to a finite von Neumann algebra would require a compatible positive ridge representation and the corresponding integrability and comparison identities; it is a further problem beyond the real-directional matrix and compact Schatten results proved here.

Theorem C.1.
  1. (1)

Appendix D Analytic regularization and its nonsharp background

The operator 𝒯ℬ\mathcal{T}_{\mathcal{B}} and its real-part identities are given in (C.2). Write ℋℬ=−i⁡(𝒯ℬ−I)\mathcal{H}_{\mathcal{B}}=-i(\mathcal{T}_{\mathcal{B}}-I) for conjugation. The three orthogonal components in (C.1) give

ℋℬ2=−I+Φ,Φ​ℋℬ=0,‖ℋℬ​x‖2≤‖x‖2.\mathcal{H}_{\mathcal{B}}^{2}=-I+\Phi,\qquad\Phi\mathcal{H}_{\mathcal{B}}=0,\qquad\|\mathcal{H}_{\mathcal{B}}x\|_{2}\leq\|x\|_{2}.

For self-adjoint gg, ℋℬ​g\mathcal{H}_{\mathcal{B}}g is self-adjoint and 𝒯ℬ​g=g+i​ℋℬ​g\mathcal{T}_{\mathcal{B}}g=g+i\mathcal{H}_{\mathcal{B}}g. The following auxiliary estimates justify analytic regularization independently of the sharp theorem. The moment estimate first puts the powers of the canonical element in H1H^{1}. Yosida approximation then identifies their exponential series with the contraction semigroup, establishing analytic resolvent membership before any sharp LpL^{p} estimate is used.

D.1. A nonsharp moment estimate used only for regularization

Lemma D.1.

For dyadic q=2nq=2^{n}, n≥1n\geq 1, the conjugation satisfies

‖v‖2​q2≤2​‖u‖2​q2+2​Cq​‖u‖2​q​‖v‖2​q.\|v\|_{2q}^{2}\leq 2\|u\|_{2q}^{2}+2C_{q}\|u\|_{2q}\|v\|_{2q}.

D.2. Bounded analytic accretive approximants: a proof

We use the standard maximally accretive semigroup theorem in its usual operator form: a maximally accretive operator AA generates a contraction semigroup e−t​Ae^{-tA}, its resolvent is the Laplace integral of that semigroup, and its bounded Yosida approximants An=A​(I+A/n)−1A_{n}=A(I+A/n)^{-1} have semigroups converging strongly to it. These statements are the Lumer–Phillips theorem, the Laplace resolvent formula, and the Yosida approximation theorem; see [30, Theorems II.3.15, II.1.10 and Section III.4.10]. They are independent of Hardy or Riesz bounds. The following proof establishes all the analytic membership and approximation assertions needed here.

Lemma D.2.

Let g∈ℳg\in\mathcal{M} be bounded and positive and put h=𝒯ℬ​gh=\mathcal{T}_{\mathcal{B}}g, d=Φ​gd=\Phi g. For every ε>0\varepsilon>0,

Rε=(I+ε​h)−1∈ℬ,‖Rε‖∞≤1,R_{\varepsilon}=(I+\varepsilon h)^{-1}\in\mathcal{B},\qquad\|R_{\varepsilon}\|_{\infty}\leq 1,

and

bε=h​Rε∈ℬ,Re⁡bε≥0,Φ​bε=d​(I+ε​d)−1≥0.b_{\varepsilon}=hR_{\varepsilon}\in\mathcal{B},\qquad\operatorname{Re}b_{\varepsilon}\geq 0,\qquad\Phi b_{\varepsilon}=d(I+\varepsilon d)^{-1}\geq 0.

Moreover bε→hb_{\varepsilon}\to h in L2L^{2}, and hence in LsL^{s} for 1<s<21<s<2, while Re⁡bε→g\operatorname{Re}b_{\varepsilon}\to g in the same spaces.

Proof.

Put K=ℋℬ​gK=\mathcal{H}_{\mathcal{B}}g, viewed as a self-adjoint affiliated operator, and realize h=g+i​Kh=g+iK on Dom⁡K\operatorname{Dom}K. Since gg is bounded, hh is closed and h∗=g−i​Kh^{*}=g-iK on the same domain. Both operators are accretive. For λ>‖g‖∞\lambda>\|g\|_{\infty}, the factorization

λ+h=[I+g​(λ+i​K)−1]​(λ+i​K)\lambda+h=[I+g(\lambda+iK)^{-1}](\lambda+iK)

is onto by a Neumann series, since ‖g​(λ+i​K)−1‖≤‖g‖∞/λ<1\|g(\lambda+iK)^{-1}\|\leq\|g\|_{\infty}/\lambda<1. Thus hh, and likewise h∗h^{*}, is maximally accretive. Affiliation and uniqueness of the generated semigroup imply that its resolvents and contraction semigroup commute with every unitary in the commutant and hence belong to ℳ\mathcal{M}. In particular, ‖(I+ε​h)−1‖≤1\|(I+\varepsilon h)^{-1}\|\leq 1.

We prove that its contraction semigroup St=e−t​hS_{t}=e^{-th} lies in ℬ\mathcal{B}. By (D.1), for 0<t<(2​e​‖g‖∞)−10<t<(2e\|g\|_{\infty})^{-1} the formal series

∑k=0∞(−t)k​hkk!\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\frac{(-t)^{k}h^{k}}{k!}

converges in H1H^{1}: the estimate k!≥(k/e)kk!\geq(k/e)^{k} makes its norm majorant geometric. If g=0g=0, the assertion is immediate instead. To identify the series, let Rn=(I+h/n)−1R_{n}=(I+h/n)^{-1} and hn=h​Rnh_{n}=hR_{n}. The bounded Yosida semigroups e−t​hne^{-th_{n}} converge strongly to StS_{t} and are contractions. Resolvents commute with hh on its domain, so in the algebra of measurable operators

hnk=hk​Rnk,‖hnk‖1≤‖hk‖1.h_{n}^{k}=h^{k}R_{n}^{k},\qquad\|h_{n}^{k}\|_{1}\leq\|h^{k}\|_{1}.

Both hh and h∗h^{*} are maximally accretive, so Rn→IR_{n}\to I strongly and Rn∗→IR_{n}^{*}\to I strongly. Therefore bounded multiplier convergence gives hnk→hkh_{n}^{k}\to h^{k} in L1L^{1} for every fixed kk. This multiplier convergence follows directly by truncating a fixed L1L^{1} element to bounded operators and using the finite trace. Dominated convergence of the exponential series therefore gives convergence in L1L^{1} to the displayed H1H^{1} series. Strong convergence of the uniformly bounded semigroups, applied to the identity vector in the standard L2L^{2} representation, also gives convergence in L2L^{2} and hence L1L^{1} to StS_{t}. Consequently St∈H1∩ℳ=ℬS_{t}\in H^{1}\cap\mathcal{M}=\mathcal{B} for small positive tt. The semigroup law then yields St∈ℬS_{t}\in\mathcal{B} for all t>0t>0.

The resolvent formula

Rε=∫0∞e−t​Sε​t​𝑑tR_{\varepsilon}=\int_{0}^{\infty}e^{-t}S_{\varepsilon t}\,dt

now shows Rε∈ℬR_{\varepsilon}\in\mathcal{B}, since ℬ\mathcal{B} is ultraweakly closed and the integrand has norm at most e−te^{-t}. The identity bε=h​Rε=(I−Rε)/εb_{\varepsilon}=hR_{\varepsilon}=(I-R_{\varepsilon})/\varepsilon shows that bεb_{\varepsilon} is bounded and analytic. Multiplicativity extends to a bounded analytic factor times an H2H^{2} factor by L2L^{2} approximation. Applying it to Rε​(I+ε​h)=IR_{\varepsilon}(I+\varepsilon h)=I gives

Φ​Rε=(I+ε​d)−1,Φ​bε=d​(I+ε​d)−1≥0.\Phi R_{\varepsilon}=(I+\varepsilon d)^{-1},\qquad\Phi b_{\varepsilon}=d(I+\varepsilon d)^{-1}\geq 0.

Using (I+ε​h)​Rε=I(I+\varepsilon h)R_{\varepsilon}=I and Re⁡h=g\operatorname{Re}h=g gives the bounded quadratic-form identity

Re⁡bε=Rε∗​g​Rε+ε​bε∗​bε≥0.\operatorname{Re}b_{\varepsilon}=R_{\varepsilon}^{*}gR_{\varepsilon}+\varepsilon b_{\varepsilon}^{*}b_{\varepsilon}\geq 0.

All terms are bounded since gg and bεb_{\varepsilon} are bounded. Finally Rε,Rε∗→IR_{\varepsilon},R_{\varepsilon}^{*}\to I strongly. Uniform boundedness and truncation of h∈L2h\in L^{2} give bε=h​Rε→hb_{\varepsilon}=hR_{\varepsilon}\to h in L2L^{2}, and taking real parts gives the remaining convergence assertions. ∎

Appendix E Rotations and independent coordinates

The real-pencil and joint realization theorems have further consequences obtained by rotation and by iteration over independent variables. We record the full statements, including one-component Schatten membership and the canonical completely bounded norms.

Corollary E.1.

Let (c,d)≠(0,0)(c,d)\neq(0,0). The optimal constant, uniform over finite nilpotent T=A+i​BT=A+iB, in ‖a​A+b​B‖p≤L​‖c​A+d​B‖p\|aA+bB\|_{p}\leq L\|cA+dB\|_{p} is

(E.1) L=Kp​(a​c+b​dc2+d2,b​c−a​dc2+d2).L=K_{p}\left(\frac{ac+bd}{c^{2}+d^{2}},\frac{bc-ad}{c^{2}+d^{2}}\right).

The same bound holds for compact quasinilpotent T∈𝒮pT\in\mathcal{S}_{p}. It also holds if TT is compact and quasinilpotent and only c​A+d​B∈𝒮pcA+dB\in\mathcal{S}_{p} is assumed.

Proof.

Put r=c2+d2r=\sqrt{c^{2}+d^{2}} and rotate TT so that its self-adjoint parts are A′=(c​A+d​B)/rA^{\prime}=(cA+dB)/r and B′=(−d​A+c​B)/rB^{\prime}=(-dA+cB)/r. Then a​A+b​B=((a​c+b​d)/r)​A′+((b​c−a​d)/r)​B′aA+bB=((ac+bd)/r)A^{\prime}+((bc-ad)/r)B^{\prime}. Corollary 1.5 and homogeneity prove the formula. The rotation bijects the class of finite nilpotents, so sharpness transfers in both directions. If c​A+d​B=0cA+dB=0 for a nilpotent TT, the rotated operator is skew-Hermitian and nilpotent and hence zero. The weaker membership assumption follows from the qualitative Matsaev theorem [21, 23, 24], applied to ii times the rotated operator. ∎

Corollary E.2.

For 1≤j≤d1\leq j\leq d, let Ωj\Omega_{j} be ℝ\mathbb{R} with Lebesgue measure or ℤ\mathbb{Z} with counting measure. Let 𝐒j=(Sj,k)k=1mj\mathbf{S}_{j}=(S_{j,k})_{k=1}^{m_{j}} be respectively a joint Hilbert-pencil family or a shifted discrete family from Theorem 1.4, with common norm LjL_{j}. Put Ω=∏jΩj\Omega=\prod_{j}\Omega_{j}, m=∏jmjm=\prod_{j}m_{j}, and

𝐒=(∏j=1dSj,kj(j))k1,…,kd.\mathbf{S}=\left(\prod_{j=1}^{d}S_{j,k_{j}}^{(j)}\right)_{k_{1},\ldots,k_{d}}.

For every nonzero Hilbert space 𝒦\mathcal{K}, this map from Lp​(Ω,𝒮p​(𝒦))L^{p}(\Omega;\mathcal{S}_{p}(\mathcal{K})) to ℓpm​(Lp​(Ω,𝒮p​(𝒦)))\ell_{p}^{m}(L^{p}(\Omega;\mathcal{S}_{p}(\mathcal{K}))) has norm ∏jLj\prod_{j}L_{j}. Its scalar and canonical completely bounded scalar norms have the same value. For unweighted single-output families, Lj=Kp​(aj,bj)L_{j}=K_{p}(a_{j},b_{j}) on ℝ\mathbb{R} and Lj=Kp​(cos⁡(π​αj),sin⁡(π​αj))L_{j}=K_{p}(\cos(\pi\alpha_{j}),\sin(\pi\alpha_{j})) on ℤ\mathbb{Z}.

Proof.

Apply each one-coordinate estimate to the corresponding slices, and sum the other coordinates and output indices by Fubini–Tonelli. Iteration gives the upper product bound, equally for mixed discrete and continuous coordinates. Products of scalar approximate extremizers, multiplied by a fixed rank-one projection, give the lower bound because both input and joint output norms factor. A zero factor is immediate. The same estimates hold for every 𝒮pn\mathcal{S}_{p}^{n} coefficient space, so Lemma 4.6 gives the complete norm equality. ∎
